name: Apple cider vinegar whitening

lead: Apple cider vinegar whitening means rinsing the mouth with ACV to lift stains and brighten the teeth. It is a common natural-remedy suggestion.

Proponents say acetic acid dissolves stains and kills bacteria. ACV is roughly 5% acetic acid and also contains malic acid. No clinical trials of this use were found, and acids can also dissolve tooth mineral.

paras: People swish diluted or undiluted ACV around the mouth briefly, or apply it to the teeth, then rinse with water. It is used occasionally as a natural add-on to normal brushing. Users describe a cleaner feel and report gradual brightening.
Enamel erosion is irreversible and can expose sensitive dentin. Dental sources note that frequency of acid exposure matters and that brushing immediately after acid is discouraged.

angle.text: Users swish apple cider vinegar as a natural rinse to dissolve stain and brighten teeth, crediting its acetic acid. It is a low-cost kitchen routine for a whiter-looking smile. No trials of it as a whitener exist, and reference sources list enamel erosion as a known risk of excessive vinegar intake.

lead: Apple cider vinegar (ACV) whitening is a home practice of swishing diluted or undiluted apple cider vinegar around the mouth, or applying it to the teeth, in the hope of removing stains. It is circulated as a natural whitening rinse.

ACV is roughly 5% acetic acid and also contains malic acid [1]. Its listed risks include tooth enamel erosion and increased dentin sensitivity with excessive intake [1]. No clinical trials of ACV as a tooth whitener were found.

paras: Users describe gargling or rinsing with ACV, sometimes diluted in water, and sometimes followed by brushing. Proponents argue that its acidity dissolves stains, and some credit its antibacterial reputation. Health organizations and regulators do not recommend ACV as a therapy, and there is no high-quality clinical evidence for its other popular health claims [1].
No studies found. A 2020 systematic review of ACV consumption generally found diluted, moderate intake appeared safe, but it was not a study of tooth whitening [1].

Dental erosion is described as irreversible loss of tooth structure by non-bacterial acid. Items with pH below roughly 5 to 5.7 can trigger it, vinegar-pickled foods are implicated, and swishing acidic liquids increases widespread erosion [2]. Dentin hypersensitivity can follow when acid wears away enamel and exposes dentin; guidance includes not brushing immediately after acid exposure [3].
For comparison, peroxide whitening itself commonly causes sensitivity, and enamel surface changes have been reported [4].
ACV is among the natural whitening routines shared online. No community-sourced material was available for citation here.
